question_html: Under explanation (ii) to section 43, preference share capital is that part of a company's issued share capital which carries a preferential right in respect of which two matters?

options.A: Payment of dividend (either an absolute amount or an amount calculated at a fixed rate) and repayment of capital in the case of winding up or repayment of capital
options.B: Payment of dividend only, with no preferential right at all in respect of repayment of capital on winding up
options.C: Voting on every resolution placed before the company and repayment of capital in the case of winding up
options.D: Appointment of directors to the Board and repayment of capital in the case of winding up

answer_html:
Correct answer: (A) Payment of dividend (either an absolute amount or an amount calculated at a fixed rate) and repayment of capital in the case of winding up or repayment of capital

Explanation (ii) to section 43 defines preference share capital as carrying a preferential right as to: (a) payment of dividend (an absolute amount or an amount calculated at a fixed rate, which may be free of or subject to income-tax), and (b) repayment of capital in the case of winding up or repayment of capital - and this preference exists only up to the amount paid up or deemed to have been paid up.

question_html: Can a company limited by shares have only preference share capital, with no equity share capital at all?

options.A: Yes - a company may freely choose to have only preference share capital, provided its articles expressly authorise this structure
options.B: No - a company may have only equity share capital, but it cannot have only preference share capital, because preference shareholders have certain preferential rights over equity shareholders, and in the absence of equity share capital there can be no such 'preference'
options.C: Yes, provided the company is a private company rather than a public company
options.D: No, but only because SEBI regulations prohibit companies with only preference share capital from being listed

answer_html:
Correct answer: (B) No - a company may have only equity share capital, but it cannot have only preference share capital, because preference shareholders have certain preferential rights over equity shareholders, and in the absence of equity share capital there can be no such 'preference'

A company may have only equity share capital, but cannot have only preference share capital - since preference shareholders' rights are defined relative to and preferential over equity shareholders, the very concept of 'preference' share capital presupposes the existence of equity share capital.

question_html: Under section 43(a) read with explanation (i) thereto, equity share capital (share capital which is not preference share capital) is further classified into which two categories?

options.A: Equity shares held by promoters and equity shares held by the general public, this being the sole basis of classification recognised under section 43(a)
options.B: Equity shares issued for cash and equity shares issued for consideration other than cash, this being the sole basis of classification recognised under section 43(a)

question_html: Under section 46(1), what evidentiary status does a duly issued share certificate (specifying the shares held by a person) have in relation to that person's title to the shares?

options.A: It is conclusive and irrebuttable proof of the person's title to such shares, admitting of no evidence to the contrary under any circumstances
options.B: It has no evidentiary value whatsoever, title to shares being provable only through the Register of Members and never through a certificate
options.C: It is merely a negotiable instrument transferable by delivery, and creates no evidentiary presumption as to title at all
options.D: It is prima facie evidence of the title of the person to such shares

answer_html:
Correct answer: (D) It is prima facie evidence of the title of the person to such shares

Section 46(1) provides that a share certificate, issued under the company's common seal (if any) or signed by two directors (or a director and company secretary), specifying the shares held by a person, is prima facie evidence of that person's title to the shares - a rebuttable, not conclusive, presumption.

question_html: Under section 46(5), if a company issues a duplicate certificate of shares with intent to defraud, what is the minimum fine that may be imposed on the company?

options.A: A fine not less than five times the face value of the shares involved in the issue of the duplicate certificate (subject to a maximum of the higher of ten times the face value of such shares, or rupees ten crore)
options.B: A fine not less than rupees one lakh, subject to a maximum of rupees ten lakh, regardless of the face value of the shares involved
options.C: A fine not less than the face value of the shares involved, with no prescribed maximum under section 46(5)
options.D: A fixed penalty of rupees fifty thousand, irrespective of the number or face value of the shares involved

answer_html:
Correct answer: (A) A fine not less than five times the face value of the shares involved in the issue of the duplicate certificate (subject to a maximum of the higher of ten times the face value of such shares, or rupees ten crore)

Section 46(5) prescribes that a company issuing a duplicate share certificate with intent to defraud is punishable with a fine of not less than five times the face value of the shares involved, extending up to the higher of ten times the face value of such shares or Rs. 10 crore; every officer in default is separately liable to action under section 447.

question_html: Under section 47(1), every member of a company limited by shares holding equity share capital has a right to vote on every resolution placed before the company, and on a poll, in what proportion is his voting right exercised?

options.A: In proportion to the number of shares held by him, irrespective of whether those shares are fully or partly paid-up
options.B: Equally with every other equity shareholder, on a strict one-member-one-vote basis regardless of shareholding
options.C: In proportion to his share in the paid-up equity share capital of the company
options.D: In proportion to the nominal (face) value of the total authorised equity share capital of the company

answer_html:
Correct answer: (C) In proportion to his share in the paid-up equity share capital of the company

Section 47(1)(b) provides that a member's voting right on a poll shall be in proportion to his share in the paid-up equity share capital of the company - not merely the number of shares held, which is relevant where shares are partly paid.

question_html: Under the second proviso to section 47(2), when does a preference shareholder become entitled to vote on all resolutions placed before the company (and not merely those directly affecting his class rights, or winding up/reduction of capital)?

options.A: Where the preference shareholder holds shares having an aggregate face value exceeding rupees one crore
options.B: Where the preference shares held by him are listed on a recognised stock exchange, irrespective of any default in dividend payment
options.C: Where the preference shareholder has held his shares continuously for a period exceeding five years
options.D: Where the dividend in respect of his class of preference shares has not been paid for a period of two years or more

answer_html:
Correct answer: (D) Where the dividend in respect of his class of preference shares has not been paid for a period of two years or more

The second proviso to section 47(2) grants a preference shareholder the right to vote on all resolutions placed before the company where dividend on his class of preference shares has remained unpaid for two years or more - since preference dividend is presumed cumulative unless the articles clearly exclude cumulation.

question_html: Under the first proviso to section 47(2), where both equity shareholders and preference shareholders are entitled to vote on a resolution, in what proportion is the voting right of equity shareholders to that of preference shareholders determined?

options.A: In the same proportion as the paid-up capital in respect of the equity shares bears to the paid-up capital in respect of the preference shares
options.B: In the fixed statutory proportion of 1:1, regardless of the relative paid-up capital of the two classes

options.A: The holders of at least 51% of the issued shares of that class must give their consent in writing, this being the ordinary-resolution threshold
options.B: The holders of at least 75% of the issued shares of that class must give their consent in writing, or a special resolution sanctioning the variation must be passed at a separate class meeting

question_html: Under section 48(2), what right is available to dissenting shareholders after a variation of class rights has been consented to/approved, and within what time limit must it be exercised?

options.A: Holders of at least 50% of the shares of that class who did not consent may apply to the Tribunal, within a period of six months after the date the consent was given or the resolution was passed
options.B: Any single dissenting shareholder, irrespective of his shareholding, may apply to the Tribunal at any time without a prescribed limitation period

options.A: A change in the rate of dividend payable on a class of preference shares from a fixed rate to a floating rate linked to a benchmark
options.B: A change in the priority of a class of preference shares' right to repayment of capital on winding up, relative to another class
options.C: A change from cumulative to non-cumulative preference dividend for an existing class of preference shares
options.D: A new issue of preference shares ranking pari-passu with existing preference shares, and cancellation of shares / reduction of capital

answer_html:
Correct answer: (D) A new issue of preference shares ranking pari-passu with existing preference shares, and cancellation of shares / reduction of capital

Per White v. Bristol Aeroplane Co Ltd and Essar Steel Ltd, re, a new issue of preference shares ranking pari-passu with existing shares does not amount to a variation requiring class consent, and cancellation of shares/reduction of capital likewise does not amount to variation of class rights.

question_html: Under section 49, calls on shares falling under the same class must be made on what basis, and what is a key exception noted regarding what constitutes 'the same class'?

options.A: Calls must be made on a uniform basis on all shares falling under the same class; but shares of the same nominal value on which different sums have already been paid are NOT deemed, for this purpose, to fall under the same class
options.B: Calls may be made on a differential basis within the same class of shares, at the sole discretion of the Board of Directors, with no requirement of uniformity
options.C: Calls must be made on a uniform basis across ALL classes of shares issued by the company, without regard to differences in nominal value or amount paid-up
options.D: Calls may be made selectively on some members of a class only, provided the Board records reasons in the minutes of its meeting

answer_html:
Correct answer: (A) Calls must be made on a uniform basis on all shares falling under the same class; but shares of the same nominal value on which different sums have already been paid are NOT deemed, for this purpose, to fall under the same class

Section 49 requires calls to be made on a uniform basis on shares of the same class - but shares of the same nominal value on which different sums have been paid are not treated as being of the same class for this purpose (they are, in effect, different classes for call purposes).

question_html: Under section 50, if a company (authorised by its articles) accepts an advance payment of the whole or part of the amount remaining unpaid on shares before any call is made, does such advance payment entitle the paying member to additional voting rights compared to other members?

options.A: Yes - the member acquires full voting rights in proportion to the total amount paid (including the advance), immediately upon making the advance payment
options.B: No - such advance payment does not entitle the member to any additional voting rights as compared with other members, until the amount is actually called up by the company
options.C: Yes, but only if the articles specifically state that advance payments carry voting rights equivalent to a fully paid-up share
options.D: No such restriction exists under section 50; voting rights always accrue immediately and automatically upon any payment actually received by the company

answer_html:
Correct answer: (B) No - such advance payment does not entitle the member to any additional voting rights as compared with other members, until the amount is actually called up by the company

Section 50 permits calls-in-advance if authorised by the articles, but expressly clarifies that such advance payment does not confer additional voting rights on the paying member as compared with other members, until the amount is actually called up by the company in the ordinary course.

question_html: Under section 51, if authorised by its articles, how may a company pay dividends where its equity shares are not equally paid-up?

options.A: The company must pay an identical dividend per share to every equity shareholder, irrespective of the amount paid-up on each share, regardless of what the articles provide
options.B: The company is statutorily barred from paying any dividend at all until every equity share is fully paid-up
options.C: The company may pay dividends in proportion to the amount paid-up on each share (i.e., on a pro rata basis)
options.D: The company may pay dividend only to shareholders holding fully paid-up shares, entirely excluding shareholders holding partly paid-up shares from any dividend

answer_html:
Correct answer: (C) The company may pay dividends in proportion to the amount paid-up on each share (i.e., on a pro rata basis)

Section 51 permits a company (if so authorised by its articles) to pay dividends in proportion to the amount paid-up on each share, where not all equity shares are equally paid-up - the Board may decide to pay dividend on a pro rata basis in such a case. (Preference shares, by contrast, are always paid dividend at a fixed rate.)

question_html: Under section 52(2), for which of the following purposes may a company apply its Securities Premium Account?

options.A: For payment of dividend to equity shareholders in a year in which the company has inadequate distributable profits, treating the premium account as a free reserve for that limited purpose
options.B: For repayment of unsecured trade payables owed to the company's ordinary suppliers in the usual course of business
options.C: For payment of remuneration to managerial personnel in excess of the limits otherwise prescribed under the Companies Act, 2013
options.D: For issue of fully paid bonus shares, writing off preliminary expenses, writing off issue expenses (including commission/discount on any issue of shares or debentures), premium payable on redemption of preference shares or debentures, and buy-back under section 68

Correct answer: (D) For issue of fully paid bonus shares, writing off preliminary expenses, writing off issue expenses (including commission/discount on any issue of shares or debentures), premium payable on redemption of preference shares or debentures, and buy-back under section 68

question_html: Under section 53(2), what is the legal status of any share issued by a company at a discount, in contravention of section 53(1)?

options.A: Any share issued at a discount by the company is void
options.B: Any share issued at a discount is voidable at the option of the company alone, and remains valid and binding unless and until the company itself elects to avoid it
options.C: Any share issued at a discount is valid and fully binding, subject only to payment of a penalty by the company and its officers under section 53(3)
options.D: Any share issued at a discount automatically converts, by operation of law, into a sweat equity share issued under section 54

answer_html:
Correct answer: (A) Any share issued at a discount by the company is void

Section 53(2) provides that any share issued by a company at a discount (otherwise than as permitted, e.g., sweat equity shares under section 54, or the section 53(2A) creditor-to-shares conversion route) is void. Section 53(3) additionally imposes penalties: the company must refund monies received with 12% p.a. interest, and every officer in default is liable to a penalty up to the lesser of the amount raised through the discounted issue or Rs. 5 lakh.

question_html: Do the restrictions contained in sections 52 (securities premium) and 53 (prohibition on discount) apply to the pricing of debt instruments such as bonds or debentures?

options.A: Yes - sections 52 and 53 apply equally and without distinction to the issue of shares, bonds, and debentures alike
options.B: No - the restrictions in sections 52 and 53 apply only to the issue of shares (equity or preference), and not to debt-related instruments like bonds or debentures, whose pricing is mostly governed by yield-to-maturity (YTM) considerations
options.C: Yes, but only in the case of secured debentures; unsecured debentures remain outside the scope of sections 52 and 53
options.D: No, but only because bonds and debentures are excluded from the definition of 'securities' under the Companies Act, 2013

answer_html:
Correct answer: (B) No - the restrictions in sections 52 and 53 apply only to the issue of shares (equity or preference), and not to debt-related instruments like bonds or debentures, whose pricing is mostly governed by yield-to-maturity (YTM) considerations

Sections 52 and 53 apply only to the issue of shares (equity or preference) - debt instruments like bonds and debentures fall outside their scope, since debt pricing is governed by yield-to-maturity (YTM) and market considerations rather than the 'premium/discount to face value' framework applicable to shares.

question_html: Under section 2(88), 'sweat equity shares' means equity shares issued by a company to its directors or employees, at a discount or for consideration other than cash, for what purpose?

options.A: Solely as a reward for long service, calculated strictly on the basis of the number of years the director or employee has been associated with the company
options.B: Solely in lieu of, and as a substitute for, the cash salary or wages that would otherwise be payable to the director or employee under his contract of employment

Section 2(88) defines sweat equity shares as equity shares issued to directors or employees at a discount or for non-cash consideration, for providing know-how, making available IPR-type rights, or value additions, by whatever name called - distinct from an Employee Stock Option, and not issuable in lieu of ordinary remuneration.

question_html: Under Rule 8(4) of the Companies (Share Capital and Debentures) Rules, 2014, during a year, what is the maximum amount for which a company (other than a start-up) may issue sweat equity shares?

options.A: A fixed statutory limit of Rs. 1 crore per year, irrespective of the company's paid-up equity share capital
options.B: The lower of 15% of the existing paid-up equity share capital, or shares of issue value of Rs. 5 crore
options.C: 25% of the paid-up equity share capital of the company per year, with no alternative fixed rupee threshold
options.D: The higher of 15% of the existing paid-up equity share capital, or shares of issue value of Rs. 5 crore

question_html: Under section 55, can a company limited by shares issue irredeemable preference shares, and what is the maximum tenor within which redeemable preference shares must ordinarily be redeemed?

options.A: Yes, a company limited by shares may freely issue irredeemable preference shares, there being no statutory bar under the Companies Act, 2013
options.B: No, a company limited by shares cannot issue irredeemable preference shares; redeemable preference shares must ordinarily be redeemed within a period not exceeding twenty years from the date of issue
options.C: No irredeemable preference shares may be issued, but redeemable preference shares must be redeemed within a period not exceeding five years from the date of issue in every case, without exception
options.D: Yes, a company limited by shares may issue irredeemable preference shares, provided its articles expressly authorise such an issue

answer_html:
Correct answer: (B) No, a company limited by shares cannot issue irredeemable preference shares; redeemable preference shares must ordinarily be redeemed within a period not exceeding twenty years from the date of issue

Section 55(1) bars issue of irredeemable preference shares by a company limited by shares (a bar introduced by the 1988 amendment to the Companies Act, 1956). Section 55(2) caps the ordinary tenor of redeemable preference shares at 20 years from issue, subject to the infrastructure-project exception (up to 30 years, with mandatory annual redemption of at least 10% from the 21st year onwards).

question_html: Where preference shares are redeemed out of the profits of the company (otherwise available for dividend), what amount must be transferred to the Capital Redemption Reserve, and is this amount affected by any premium paid on redemption?

options.A: A sum equal to the total amount actually paid to preference shareholders on redemption, including any premium, must be transferred to the Capital Redemption Reserve
options.B: No amount at all needs to be transferred to any reserve where preference shares are redeemed out of profits, this requirement applying only where redemption is funded through a fresh issue of shares
options.C: A sum equal to the NOMINAL AMOUNT of the shares to be redeemed must be transferred to the Capital Redemption Reserve out of such profits; no amount paid towards premium on redemption needs to be transferred to the CRR account
options.D: A sum equal to twice the nominal amount of the shares to be redeemed must be transferred to the Capital Redemption Reserve, to provide an adequate margin of safety for creditors

answer_html:
Correct answer: (C) A sum equal to the NOMINAL AMOUNT of the shares to be redeemed must be transferred to the Capital Redemption Reserve out of such profits; no amount paid towards premium on redemption needs to be transferred to the CRR account

The second proviso to section 55(2) requires transfer to the CRR of a sum equal to the NOMINAL AMOUNT of the shares redeemed (out of profits otherwise available for dividend) - premium (if any) payable on redemption is separately sourced (out of profits or the securities premium account, as applicable) and does NOT need to be transferred to the CRR.

question_html: Under section 55(3), where a company is unable to redeem preference shares (or pay dividend on them) in accordance with the terms of issue, what course of action is available to it?

options.A: It may unilaterally extend the redemption date by up to five years through a Board resolution alone, without requiring shareholder consent or Tribunal approval
options.B: It must compulsorily wind up voluntarily within six months of the default in redemption, this being the sole remedy available under section 55(3)
options.C: It may convert the unredeemed preference shares into equity shares at par value, without requiring the consent of the preference shareholders or Tribunal approval
options.D: It may issue further redeemable preference shares equal to the amount due (including dividend thereon) to the holders of the unredeemed preference shares, with the consent of holders of three-fourths in value of such unredeemed preference shares and the approval of the Tribunal on a petition made in this behalf

answer_html:
Correct answer: (D) It may issue further redeemable preference shares equal to the amount due (including dividend thereon) to the holders of the unredeemed preference shares, with the consent of holders of three-fourths in value of such unredeemed preference shares and the approval of the Tribunal on a petition made in this behalf

Section 55(3) permits a company unable to redeem preference shares (or pay dividend thereon) to issue further redeemable preference shares equal to the amount due (with dividend), with the consent of holders of 3/4th in value of the unredeemed preference shares and Tribunal approval on petition - upon which the unredeemed shares are deemed redeemed. The Tribunal must order forthwith redemption of shares held by non-consenting holders.

question_html: Under section 56(1), which of the following is a condition that must be fulfilled before a company registers a transfer of securities held in physical form?

options.A: The instrument of transfer must be executed by both the transferor and transferee, specify the transferee's name/address/occupation, be duly stamped and dated, be in the prescribed form (Form SH-4), and be delivered to the company (with the relevant share certificate/letter of allotment) within 60 days from the date of execution
options.B: It is sufficient that the transferee alone signs the instrument of transfer, there being no requirement for the transferor's signature under section 56(1)
options.C: It is sufficient that the transfer is orally communicated to the company by either the transferor or the transferee, with no requirement for a written or stamped instrument
options.D: It is sufficient that the transfer is recorded in the company's internal records within any period the Board considers reasonable, with no fixed statutory time limit

answer_html:
Correct answer: (A) The instrument of transfer must be executed by both the transferor and transferee, specify the transferee's name/address/occupation, be duly stamped and dated, be in the prescribed form (Form SH-4), and be delivered to the company (with the relevant share certificate/letter of allotment) within 60 days from the date of execution

Section 56(1) requires: execution by both transferor and transferee, transferee particulars stated, due stamping and dating, the prescribed form (Form SH-4 under Rule 11(1)), and delivery to the company (with the share certificate or letter of allotment) within 60 days of execution - the proviso allows registration on indemnity terms if the instrument is lost or not delivered in time.

question_html: How does 'transmission' of securities differ from 'transfer' of securities, and what document is typically required for the company to register a transmission?

options.A: Transmission and transfer are legally identical concepts requiring an identically executed instrument of transfer in Form SH-4 in every case, differing only in name
options.B: Transmission means devolution of title otherwise than by transfer (e.g., by death, succession, inheritance, bankruptcy, or marriage), and is effected by forwarding necessary documents (such as a notarised death certificate or succession certificate) to the company - no instrument of transfer/transfer deed is required, since the deceased/insolvent person cannot execute one as transferor
options.C: Transmission occurs only upon voluntary sale of shares by a shareholder to a third party, whereas transfer occurs only upon involuntary devolution such as death or bankruptcy - i.e., the definitions are the reverse of their ordinary usage
options.D: Transmission requires the same 60-day delivery period and stamped instrument of transfer that governs an ordinary transfer under section 56(1), with no substantive procedural difference

answer_html:
Correct answer: (B) Transmission means devolution of title otherwise than by transfer (e.g., by death, succession, inheritance, bankruptcy, or marriage), and is effected by forwarding necessary documents (such as a notarised death certificate or succession certificate) to the company - no instrument of transfer/transfer deed is required, since the deceased/insolvent person cannot execute one as transferor

Transmission is devolution of title otherwise than by transfer (death, succession, inheritance, bankruptcy, marriage, etc.) - it is effected by forwarding necessary documents (e.g., a notarised death certificate, succession certificate) rather than an instrument of transfer, since a deceased or insolvent person cannot execute a transfer deed as transferor. Section 56(2) confirms the company's power to register transmission is unaffected by section 56(1)'s conditions for transfer.

question_html: Under section 56(4), within what period must a company deliver certificates of securities following a transfer, from the date of receipt of the instrument of transfer?

options.A: Within a period of two months from the date of receipt of the instrument of transfer, mirroring the period applicable to a fresh allotment of shares
options.B: Within a period of six months from the date of receipt of the instrument of transfer, mirroring the period applicable to allotment of debentures

question_html: Under section 57, a person who deceitfully personates as the owner of a security (or a share warrant/coupon) and thereby obtains or attempts to obtain the security, or receives or attempts to receive money due to the owner, is punishable with what penalty?

options.A: A fine only, of not less than Rs. 5 lakh extendable to Rs. 25 lakh, with no provision for imprisonment under section 57
options.B: Imprisonment only, for a term of not less than three years extendable to seven years, with no provision for a fine under section 57
options.C: A civil penalty recoverable by the company alone, equal to the value of the security personated, with no criminal sanction available under section 57
options.D: Imprisonment for a term of not less than one year (extendable to three years) and a fine of not less than Rs. 1 lakh (extendable to Rs. 5 lakh)

answer_html:
Correct answer: (D) Imprisonment for a term of not less than one year (extendable to three years) and a fine of not less than Rs. 1 lakh (extendable to Rs. 5 lakh)

Section 57 punishes deceitful personation to obtain a security/share warrant/coupon or money due to the true owner, with imprisonment of 1 to 3 years AND a fine of Rs. 1 lakh to Rs. 5 lakh - distinct from (though the gravity of the section 57 offence may be considered alongside) the general punishment for fraud under section 447 that applies to personation for acquisition of securities under section 38.

question_html: Under section 59(1), can any member of the company apply to the Tribunal for rectification of the register of members, without needing to demonstrate personal injury or prejudice?

options.A: No - only a member who can demonstrate direct, quantifiable personal financial loss arising from the register's inaccuracy has standing to apply for rectification
options.B: Yes - every shareholder has an interest in the proper maintenance of the register of members, and any member can make an application for rectification without showing any injury or prejudice to himself personally; personal grievance is not necessary for locus standi
options.C: No - only the company itself (acting through its Board of Directors) has standing to apply to the Tribunal for rectification of its own register of members
options.D: No - only the Registrar of Companies has standing to apply to the Tribunal for rectification of a company's register of members

answer_html:
Correct answer: (B) Yes - every shareholder has an interest in the proper maintenance of the register of members, and any member can make an application for rectification without showing any injury or prejudice to himself personally; personal grievance is not necessary for locus standi

Section 59(1) allows an aggrieved person, member, or the company to apply for rectification where a name is wrongly entered/omitted, or there is default/unnecessary delay in recording membership changes. Since every shareholder has an interest in the register's proper maintenance, any member may apply without needing to show personal injury or prejudice - personal grievance is not necessary for locus standi.

question_html: Among the several ways in which a limited company (having share capital and authorised by its articles) may alter its share capital under section 61(1) by passing a resolution at a general meeting, in which specific instance is the approval of the National Company Law Tribunal additionally required?

options.A: Whenever the company increases its authorised share capital by any amount, however small, regardless of whether voting percentages change
options.B: Whenever the company sub-divides its share capital into shares of a smaller amount, regardless of whether voting percentages change
options.C: Where consolidation and division of share capital into shares of a larger amount results in a change in the voting percentage of shareholders
options.D: Whenever the company converts fully paid-up shares into stock, regardless of whether voting percentages change

answer_html:
Correct answer: (C) Where consolidation and division of share capital into shares of a larger amount results in a change in the voting percentage of shareholders

Section 61(1)(b) permits consolidation and division of share capital, but where such consolidation and division results in a change in the voting percentage of shareholders, NCLT approval is additionally required - the other modes of alteration under section 61(1) (increase, sub-division, conversion to stock, cancellation) require only an ordinary resolution, with no Tribunal approval needed.

question_html: Under section 62(1)(a) read with Rule 12A, when a company offers further shares to existing equity shareholders by way of rights issue, what is the minimum period the letter of offer must specify for the offer to be accepted?

options.A: Not less than sixty days from the date of the offer, mirroring the period applicable to registration of a transfer of securities
options.B: Not less than ninety days from the date of the offer, with no maximum period prescribed under section 62(1)(a) or the rules
options.C: There is no minimum period prescribed; the company may specify any period it considers appropriate, entirely at its own discretion
options.D: Not less than seven days from the date of the offer (subject to the outer limit under section 62(1)(a) itself of not exceeding thirty days, and not less than fifteen days save as prescribed)

answer_html:
Correct answer: (D) Not less than seven days from the date of the offer (subject to the outer limit under section 62(1)(a) itself of not exceeding thirty days, and not less than fifteen days save as prescribed)

Section 62(1)(a) itself specifies the offer period shall not be less than 15 days (or such lesser number of days as prescribed) and not exceeding 30 days; Rule 12A (inserted in 2021) prescribes that this period shall not be less than seven days from the date of offer - reconciling the statutory minimum downward via the rule-making power.

question_html: Under section 62(3), does section 62 apply to an increase in subscribed capital arising from the conversion of debentures or loans into equity shares?

options.A: No - section 62 does not apply to such an increase in subscribed capital, provided the terms and conditions of such conversion were approved by the company in general meeting by special resolution, prior to the issue of the debentures or the grant of the loan
options.B: Yes - section 62 applies in full to conversion of debentures or loans into equity shares in exactly the same manner as it applies to a fresh rights issue
options.C: No, but only where the conversion is directed by the Central Government under section 62(4), and not where it arises from ordinary contractual conversion terms
options.D: Yes, but only where the debenture-holder or lender is a related party of the company within the meaning of section 188

answer_html:
Correct answer: (A) No - section 62 does not apply to such an increase in subscribed capital, provided the terms and conditions of such conversion were approved by the company in general meeting by special resolution, prior to the issue of the debentures or the grant of the loan

Section 62(3) exempts increase in subscribed capital via conversion of debentures/loans into shares from section 62's application, PROVIDED the conversion terms were approved by the company in general meeting via special resolution prior to the debenture issue/loan grant - this is a general statutory exception, not limited to Government-directed conversions under section 62(4).

question_html: Under section 63(1) and its proviso, out of which sources may a company issue fully paid-up bonus shares to its members, and which source is expressly barred?

options.A: Bonus shares may be issued out of any reserve of the company without restriction, including a revaluation reserve created upon revaluation of the company's fixed assets
options.B: Bonus shares may be issued out of free reserves (other than revaluation reserve), the securities premium account, or the capital redemption reserve account; bonus shares shall NOT be issued by capitalising reserves created by the revaluation of assets
options.C: Bonus shares may be issued only out of the current year's trading profits, and never out of accumulated free reserves, securities premium, or capital redemption reserve
options.D: Bonus shares may be issued only out of borrowed funds specifically raised for that purpose, and never out of the company's own reserves

answer_html:
Correct answer: (B) Bonus shares may be issued out of free reserves (other than revaluation reserve), the securities premium account, or the capital redemption reserve account; bonus shares shall NOT be issued by capitalising reserves created by the revaluation of assets

Section 63(1) permits bonus shares to be issued out of free reserves (excluding revaluation reserve), the securities premium account, or the capital redemption reserve account. The proviso expressly bars capitalising a revaluation reserve for this purpose, since such a reserve does not represent realised/distributable profit.

question_html: Under section 63(2), which of the following is a pre-condition a company must satisfy before it may capitalise its profits/reserves to issue fully paid-up bonus shares?

options.A: The company must have been in continuous operation and profitable for at least the preceding ten consecutive financial years, with no exception for younger companies
options.B: The company must obtain the prior approval of the National Company Law Tribunal before issuing any bonus shares, regardless of the amount involved
options.C: The company must not have defaulted in payment of interest or principal on fixed deposits/debt securities issued by it, and must not have defaulted in payment of statutory dues of employees (such as provident fund, gratuity, and bonus)
options.D: The company must have distributed at least 50% of its distributable profits as cash dividend to shareholders in the immediately preceding financial year

answer_html:
Correct answer: (C) The company must not have defaulted in payment of interest or principal on fixed deposits/debt securities issued by it, and must not have defaulted in payment of statutory dues of employees (such as provident fund, gratuity, and bonus)

Section 63(2) requires, among other conditions: authorisation by the articles, Board recommendation authorised in general meeting, no default in payment of interest/principal on fixed deposits or debt securities, no default in employees' statutory dues, all partly paid-up shares outstanding on the allotment date being made fully paid-up, and compliance with Rule 14 (no subsequent withdrawal of an announced bonus decision). There is no minimum operating-history or dividend-payout precondition.

question_html: Under section 66(1), a company limited by shares (or a company limited by guarantee having share capital) proposing to reduce its share capital must, after passing a special resolution, obtain confirmation from which authority before the reduction takes effect?

options.A: The Central Government acting directly (without any delegation to the Tribunal or Regional Director)
options.B: The Securities and Exchange Board of India, in the case of every company regardless of whether it is listed
options.C: The Reserve Bank of India, in the case of every company regardless of its sector or activity

answer_html:
Correct answer: (D) The Tribunal (National Company Law Tribunal)

Section 66(1) requires a company reducing its share capital (in any of the specified manners) to pass a special resolution AND obtain confirmation of the reduction from the Tribunal, which considers creditor representations and satisfies itself that creditor claims have been discharged/determined/secured/consented to, and that the proposed accounting treatment conforms to applicable accounting standards.

question_html: Under section 67(2), what is a public company generally prohibited from doing, whether directly or indirectly, by means of a loan, guarantee, provision of security, or otherwise?

options.A: Giving any financial assistance for the purpose of, or in connection with, a purchase or subscription made or to be made by any person of, or for, any shares in the company or in its holding company
options.B: Giving any financial assistance to its employees for any purpose whatsoever, this restriction applying uniformly regardless of the purpose of the assistance
options.C: Declaring or paying any dividend to its equity shareholders in any financial year in which the company has distributable profits
options.D: Accepting deposits from the public in any manner whatsoever, this being governed exclusively by section 67 rather than the deposit-acceptance provisions of the Act

answer_html:
Correct answer: (A) Giving any financial assistance for the purpose of, or in connection with, a purchase or subscription made or to be made by any person of, or for, any shares in the company or in its holding company

Section 67(2) prohibits a public company from giving financial assistance (directly or indirectly, by loan, guarantee, security, or otherwise) for the purchase or subscription of shares in itself or its holding company - subject to specified exceptions such as ordinary-course bank lending, approved employee share schemes, and limited employee loans under section 67(3)(c).

question_html: Under the proviso to section 68(2)(b), in what circumstance is a special resolution NOT necessary to authorise a buy-back, a Board resolution being sufficient instead?

options.A: Where the buy-back does not exceed 25% of the total paid-up equity capital and free reserves of the company, a Board resolution being sufficient up to this higher threshold
options.B: Where the buy-back is not exceeding 10% of the total paid-up equity capital and free reserves of the company, and such buy-back has been authorised by a Board resolution passed at its meeting
options.C: A special resolution is always mandatorily required for every buy-back under section 68, with no exception permitting a Board resolution alone, regardless of the amount involved
options.D: Where the buy-back is funded entirely out of the proceeds of a fresh issue of the same kind of shares, a Board resolution being sufficient regardless of the amount involved

answer_html:
Correct answer: (B) Where the buy-back is not exceeding 10% of the total paid-up equity capital and free reserves of the company, and such buy-back has been authorised by a Board resolution passed at its meeting

The proviso to section 68(2)(b) dispenses with the special-resolution requirement where the buy-back does not exceed 10% of the total paid-up equity capital and free reserves of the company, and is authorised instead by a Board resolution - buy-backs exceeding this 10% threshold (up to the overall 25% cap) require a special resolution.

question_html: Under section 68(2)(c) and (d), what are the overall caps on the amount involved in a buy-back, and on the company's post-buy-back debt-to-equity ratio?

options.A: The amount involved in the buy-back shall not exceed 10% of the aggregate of paid-up capital and free reserves in any circumstance, this being an absolute, non-waivable ceiling with no separate equity-specific sub-limit
options.B: There is no statutory cap on the amount involved in a buy-back, this being left entirely to the discretion of the shareholders approving the special resolution
options.C: The amount involved in the buy-back shall not exceed 25% of the aggregate of paid-up capital and free reserves (and, for equity buy-back specifically, not more than 25% of total paid-up equity capital in any financial year); and after the buy-back, the ratio of debts (secured and unsecured) owed by the company shall not be more than twice the paid-up capital and free reserves
options.D: The post-buy-back debt-to-equity ratio must not exceed 1:1 in any case, with no power for the Central Government to prescribe a higher ratio for any class of companies

answer_html:
Correct answer: (C) The amount involved in the buy-back shall not exceed 25% of the aggregate of paid-up capital and free reserves (and, for equity buy-back specifically, not more than 25% of total paid-up equity capital in any financial year); and after the buy-back, the ratio of debts (secured and unsecured) owed by the company shall not be more than twice the paid-up capital and free reserves

Section 68(2)(c) caps the buy-back amount at 25% of aggregate paid-up capital and free reserves (with a further 25%-of-paid-up-equity-capital sub-cap for equity buy-backs in a financial year). Section 68(2)(d) caps post-buy-back debt at twice the paid-up capital and free reserves (Central Government may prescribe a higher ratio for specified classes of companies).

question_html: Under section 70(1)(c), a company is prohibited from buying back its own shares if it is in default in respect of which of the following, and when does this prohibition cease to apply?

options.A: Failure to hold its Annual General Meeting within the prescribed time, this being the sole default that triggers the prohibition under section 70(1)(c), with no other default being relevant
options.B: Any default whatsoever, however trivial, with the prohibition continuing permanently and with no provision under the Act for it ever to lapse or cease

Section 70(1)(c) bars buy-back where the company is in default of repaying deposits/interest, redeeming debentures/preference shares, paying dividend, or repaying term loans/interest to financial institutions/banks - but once the default is remedied and 3 years have elapsed since it ceased to subsist, the buy-back is no longer prohibited on that ground.

question_html: Under section 69(1), where a company purchases its own shares out of free reserves or the securities premium account (as part of a buy-back), what amount must be transferred to the Capital Redemption Reserve account?

question_html: Under section 71(4) read with the relevant rules, out of what source must a company create its Debenture Redemption Reserve (DRR) account, and for what purpose alone may the amount credited to it be utilised?

options.A: The DRR account must be created out of the company's borrowed funds specifically raised for that purpose, and may be freely utilised for any general corporate purpose at the Board's discretion
options.B: The DRR account must be created out of the profits of the company available for payment of dividend, and the amount credited to it shall not be utilised by the company except for the redemption of debentures
options.C: The DRR account must be created out of the securities premium account exclusively, and may be utilised for the redemption of both debentures and preference shares interchangeably
options.D: The DRR account must be created out of the company's revaluation reserve, and may be utilised for the redemption of debentures or the payment of dividend, at the company's option

answer_html:
Correct answer: (B) The DRR account must be created out of the profits of the company available for payment of dividend, and the amount credited to it shall not be utilised by the company except for the redemption of debentures

Section 71(4) requires a company issuing debentures to create a DRR account out of profits available for payment of dividend; the amount credited to the DRR shall not be utilised except for the redemption of debentures - specific percentage requirements and exemptions (e.g., for certain listed companies, NBFCs, and banking companies) are prescribed under Rule 18(7).

Assuming the proposed new differential-rights shares would, if issued, take Meridian Autoparts' total differential-rights voting power above 74% of total voting power, can the company proceed with the issue as proposed?

options.A: Yes - the 74% cap applies only to a company's first-ever issue of differential-rights shares, and does not constrain any subsequent issue once the initial cap has been observed
options.B: Yes - since Meridian Autoparts' articles authorise the issue and it has no subsisting defaults, the 74% cap under Rule 4(1)(c) does not apply to unlisted public companies
options.C: No - Rule 4(1)(c) caps the voting power in respect of equity shares with differential rights (including shares already issued with such rights, together with the new issue) at 74% of the total voting power of the company, so any issue that would push the aggregate above this cap is not permissible
options.D: No, but only because Meridian Autoparts is proposing an ordinary resolution rather than a special resolution, and not because of the 74% voting-power cap

answer_html:
Correct answer: (C) No - Rule 4(1)(c) caps the voting power in respect of equity shares with differential rights (including shares already issued with such rights, together with the new issue) at 74% of the total voting power of the company, so any issue that would push the aggregate above this cap is not permissible

Rule 4(1)(c) caps the aggregate voting power attributable to equity shares with differential rights - including all shares with such rights issued at any point in time - at 74% of the company's total voting power. Since the existing 68% plus the proposed new issue would exceed this cap, the proposed issue (to the extent it breaches 74%) cannot proceed.

Solstice Energy Limited has two classes of equity shares: Class-1 (ordinary voting rights) and Class-2 (differential voting rights, one vote for every five shares), comprising 80,000 issued shares of Class-2 in total. Holders of 64,000 of the 80,000 issued Class-2 shares give their written consent to the variation. Of the dissenting holders (owning the remaining 16,000 shares), holders of 7,000 shares wish to apply to the Tribunal to have the variation cancelled.

Has Solstice Energy Limited obtained sufficient consent under section 48(1) to sanction the proposed variation of Class-2 shareholders' voting rights?

options.A: No - although 80% of Class-2 shares have consented, section 48(1) requires consent from at least 75% of the NUMBER of Class-2 holders (not shares), and this has not been demonstrated
options.B: Yes - holders of 64,000 out of 80,000 issued Class-2 shares (80%) have given written consent, which exceeds the 75% threshold of issued shares of that class required under section 48(1)
options.C: No - section 48(1) requires unanimous consent of 100% of the issued shares of the class before any variation can be sanctioned
options.D: Yes, but only because Class-1 shareholders were not required to give any consent at all, there being no need to consider their position under section 48

answer_html:
Correct answer: (B) Yes - holders of 64,000 out of 80,000 issued Class-2 shares (80%) have given written consent, which exceeds the 75% threshold of issued shares of that class required under section 48(1)

Section 48(1) requires consent in writing (or a special resolution at a class meeting) from holders of at least 75% of the ISSUED SHARES of the class (not 75% of the number of holders). Here, 64,000 of 80,000 Class-2 shares (80%) have consented - comfortably exceeding the 75% threshold.

Can the dissenting Class-2 holders owning 7,000 shares validly apply to the Tribunal under section 48(2) to have the variation cancelled?

options.A: Yes - any dissenting shareholder, however few shares he holds, is automatically entitled to apply to the Tribunal under section 48(2) without any minimum shareholding threshold
options.B: Yes - since 7,000 shares represent all of the shares held by dissenting shareholders who wish to object, this alone is sufficient to meet the 10% threshold under section 48(2)

options.D: No, but only because more than 21 days have necessarily elapsed since the consent was given, and not because of any shortfall in the 10% shareholding threshold

Section 48(2) requires holders of at least 10% of the ISSUED SHARES of the class (here, 10% of 80,000 = 8,000 shares) to apply to the Tribunal for the variation to be stayed pending confirmation. question_html:
Falcon Textiles Limited, an unlisted public company, has a paid-up equity capital of Rs. 40 crore and free reserves of Rs. 60 crore (aggregate Rs. 100 crore). The Board wishes to buy back equity shares worth Rs. 9 crore, relying on a Board resolution alone (without a special resolution). Separately, in a subsequent, unrelated proposal considered a few months later (after the first buy-back offer has closed), the company wishes to buy back further equity shares worth Rs. 22 crore, this time via a special resolution passed in general meeting. Before proceeding with the second buy-back, the company files a declaration of solvency in Form SH-9 with the Registrar, verified by affidavit, signed by two directors (one of whom is the managing director), confirming that the Board has made full inquiry into the company's affairs and is satisfied the company will not be rendered insolvent for a period of 12 months from the date of the declaration.

Is Falcon Textiles Limited's first proposed buy-back (Rs. 9 crore, via Board resolution alone) valid, given the company's aggregate paid-up capital and free reserves of Rs. 100 crore?

options.A: Yes - Rs. 9 crore is less than 10% of the aggregate paid-up capital and free reserves (Rs. 100 crore, so the 10% threshold is Rs. 10 crore), so the proviso to section 68(2)(b) permits this buy-back to be authorised by a Board resolution alone, without a special resolution
options.B: No - a special resolution is always required for any buy-back irrespective of the amount involved, the Board-resolution route under section 68(2)(b) being available only to private companies
options.C: No - the Board-resolution route is available only where the buy-back does not exceed 5% (not 10%) of the aggregate paid-up capital and free reserves

What amount must Cascade Infrastructure Limited maintain in its Debenture Redemption Reserve (DRR) account in respect of its Rs. 40 crore of outstanding privately placed non-convertible debentures, given that it does not fall within any of the specifically exempted categories (listed companies, All India Financial Institutions, banking companies, or RBI/NHB-registered NBFCs/HFCs)?

options.A: No DRR is required at all, since DRR requirements apply only to listed companies and Cascade Infrastructure is unlisted
options.B: An amount equal to 10% of the outstanding debentures, i.e., Rs. 4 crore, since Cascade Infrastructure (an unlisted company outside the exempted categories) is required to maintain a DRR of 10% of outstanding debentures
options.C: An amount equal to 25% of the outstanding debentures, i.e., Rs. 10 crore, this being the uniform DRR requirement applicable to all companies without exception
options.D: An amount equal to 50% of the outstanding debentures, i.e., Rs. 20 crore, since privately placed debentures attract a materially higher DRR requirement than publicly placed debentures

answer_html:
Correct answer: (B) An amount equal to 10% of the outstanding debentures, i.e., Rs. 4 crore, since Cascade Infrastructure (an unlisted company outside the exempted categories) is required to maintain a DRR of 10% of outstanding debentures

Under Rule 18(7), an unlisted company outside the specifically exempted categories (All India Financial Institutions, banking companies, RBI-registered NBFCs, and NHB-registered HFCs, which enjoy relaxations) is required to maintain a DRR of 10% of the value of outstanding debentures - here, 10% of Rs. 40 crore = Rs. 4 crore.

Is Mr. Ashwin (a shareholder holding Rs. 2 lakh worth of shares, with no other connection to the company) eligible to be appointed as debenture trustee?

options.A: No - merely holding shares beneficially in the company (a 'beneficiary holder of shares') is itself sufficient, without more, to disqualify a person from appointment as debenture trustee under Rule 18(2)
options.B: Yes - shareholding of any amount is entirely irrelevant to debenture trustee eligibility, and only promoters, directors, KMPs, and employees are disqualified under Rule 18(2)
options.C: Yes - Rule 18(2) disqualifies a person who is a BENEFICIARY holder of shares in the company from being a debenture trustee only where he additionally falls within one of the other disqualifying categories (promoter/director/KMP/employee, indebtedness, guarantee, pecuniary relationship, relative of promoter/director/KMP); merely holding shares beneficially, without more, is itself listed as a disqualifying category under Rule 18(2)(i) - so in fact Mr. Ashwin, as a beneficiary holder of shares, IS disqualified
options.D: No, but only because Mr. Ashwin's shareholding exceeds Rs. 1 lakh; a beneficiary shareholding below that threshold would not disqualify him

answer_html:
Correct answer: (C) Yes - Rule 18(2) disqualifies a person who is a BENEFICIARY holder of shares in the company from being a debenture trustee only where he additionally falls within one of the other disqualifying categories (promoter/director/KMP/employee, indebtedness, guarantee, pecuniary relationship, relative of promoter/director/KMP); merely holding shares beneficially, without more, is itself listed as a disqualifying category under Rule 18(2)(i) - so in fact Mr. Ashwin, as a beneficiary holder of shares, IS disqualified

Mr. Ashwin, holding shares beneficially, is therefore disqualified from appointment as debenture trustee, regardless of the absence of any other connection to the company.
